distractor_explanations.Multi-tasking while listening: Assumes divided attention builds skill; splitting focus prevents the sustained attention real listening requires.
distractor_explanations.Passive listening: Treats hearing as listening; skill grows through deliberate engagement, not passive exposure to sound.
distractor_explanations.Ignoring speakers: Describes the absence of listening entirely; no skill develops when the speaker's message is never attended to.

distractor_explanations.A type of grammar: Confuses citation with a grammar category; citations document sources rather than govern sentence structure.
distractor_explanations.A title: Mistakes the citation for a document feature; a title names a work, while a citation credits its source.
distractor_explanations.A conclusion: Confuses citation with a section of an essay; citations appear wherever sources are used, not only at the end.

distractor_explanations.A quotation: Copies the author's exact words instead of restating ideas in the reader's own language.
distractor_explanations.A detailed analysis: Confuses summarizing with analyzing; a summary condenses main ideas rather than examining them in depth.
distractor_explanations.A personal opinion: Injects the reader's own judgments; a summary should faithfully reflect the text's ideas without evaluation.

distractor_explanations.It doesn't matter: Dismisses voice entirely; how a writer sounds shapes whether readers trust and engage with the argument.
distractor_explanations.Voice is only for creative writing: Limits voice to fiction; persuasive writing also relies on tone and personality to connect with readers.
distractor_explanations.Formal voice is always better: Assumes one voice fits all audiences; effective writers adjust formality to purpose and reader.

distractor_explanations.Memorize dictionaries: Proposes an impossible task; memorizing dictionary entries in isolation builds no usable word knowledge.
distractor_explanations.Avoid complex words: Lowers expectations instead of building vocabulary; students grow by encountering and using richer words.
distractor_explanations.Use thesaurus blindly: Swaps words without checking meaning or fit; synonyms carry different connotations and contexts.

distractor_explanations.They are the same: Erases the distinction entirely; verifiability is exactly what separates facts from opinions.
distractor_explanations.Opinions are always wrong: Equates subjective with false; opinions can be reasonable, they simply cannot be proven or disproven.
distractor_explanations.Facts are subjective: Reverses the definitions; facts are precisely the statements that hold independent of personal feeling.

distractor_explanations.A movie: Assumes any media qualifies; a film is primary only if it originates from the period being studied.
distractor_explanations.A textbook: Mistakes a compiled, later account for a firsthand record; textbooks summarize events after the fact.
distractor_explanations.A secondary summary: Names the opposite category; secondary sources interpret events, while primary sources record them firsthand.

distractor_explanations.It is not important: Dismisses context entirely; meaning shifts with the historical and cultural conditions surrounding a text.
distractor_explanations.Context only matters for old books: Limits context to the distant past; contemporary works also carry cultural and biographical framing.
distractor_explanations.Texts are self-contained: Assumes meaning lives on the page alone; readers' interpretations are informed by circumstances outside the text.

distractor_explanations.Skipping difficult texts: Removes the very practice students need; growth in comprehension comes from supported work with challenging material.
distractor_explanations.Reading faster: Treats speed as the remedy; racing through text worsens comprehension when the real gap is understanding.
distractor_explanations.More decoding practice: Targets a skill students already have; decoding is intact, so instruction should build meaning-making instead.

distractor_explanations.Character development: Confuses plot technique with characterization; foreshadowing concerns events to come, not how characters grow.
distractor_explanations.Setting description: Mistakes the technique for scene-building; descriptive passages may hint, but foreshadowing is the hinting itself.
distractor_explanations.A type of rhyme: Misfiles the term under sound devices; foreshadowing is a plot device, not a feature of verse.

distractor_explanations.The hero: Describes the protagonist; the antagonist stands in the lead character's way rather than driving the story.
distractor_explanations.A narrator: Confuses role in telling the story with role in it; narrators recount events, antagonists oppose the lead.
distractor_explanations.A setting: Names a story element that places the action; opposition comes from a character or force, not a location.

distractor_explanations.Because it is required: Treats imagery as a rule to obey; authors choose it for its effect on readers, not from obligation.
distractor_explanations.To confuse readers: Misreads sensory language as obstruction; imagery clarifies experience by making it vivid, not murky.
distractor_explanations.To make writing longer: Reduces imagery to padding; its sensory details serve engagement and meaning, not word count.

distractor_explanations.Reading argumentative essays only: Mistakes exposure for instruction; reading without analyzing claims and evidence builds no analytic skill.
distractor_explanations.Memorizing fallacies: Focuses on labeling errors before students can identify claims and reasoning; analysis starts with structure.
distractor_explanations.Ignoring logic: Removes the very content of argument analysis; claims, evidence, and reasoning are logical connections.

distractor_explanations.A type of poem: Misfiles the term under genre; narrative structure describes how plot unfolds, not a form of verse.
distractor_explanations.Random event ordering: Assumes events appear unordered; narrative structure is the deliberate arrangement of plot stages.
distractor_explanations.Character names: Confuses story elements with story shape; structure concerns event organization, not who appears.

distractor_explanations.Exaggeration: Defines hyperbole instead; similes compare using 'like' or 'as' rather than overstating.
distractor_explanations.Personification: Names a different device; personification grants human traits, while a simile compares two things explicitly.
distractor_explanations.Direct comparison without 'like' or 'as': Defines metaphor; similes signal the comparison explicitly with 'like' or 'as'.

distractor_explanations.Cultures don't affect reading: Denies the reader's role in meaning-making; what readers notice and value is shaped by their backgrounds.
distractor_explanations.Because texts are unclear: Blames the text rather than the reader; varied readings arise from different perspectives, not vagueness.
distractor_explanations.Because one interpretation is always rig: Contradicts the premise; if one reading were fixed, cultural variation in interpretation would not occur.

distractor_explanations.A theme: Confuses the message with the events; plot is what happens, theme is what it means.
distractor_explanations.The setting: Names where and when the story occurs; plot concerns the sequence of events themselves.
distractor_explanations.A character's name: Points to a single story element; plot is the connected chain of events, not a person in it.

distractor_explanations.All texts are the same: Erases the conventions that differ across genres; readers adjust expectations between poems and manuals.
distractor_explanations.Genre doesn't matter: Dismisses the organizing role of genre; genre signals structure and purpose that guide interpretation.
distractor_explanations.Genre only affects length: Reduces genre to size; genres differ in conventions and expectations, not merely in how long they run.

distractor_explanations.More reading time: Adds quantity without changing quality; passive habits persist no matter how long students read.
distractor_explanations.Reading silently: Confuses quiet reading with engaged reading; silence alone does not produce interaction with the text.
distractor_explanations.Reading faster: Speeds up disengagement; comprehension grows from marking and questioning text, not from pace.

distractor_explanations.A character trait: Confuses who someone is with what happens; conflict is the struggle between forces, not a personality feature.
distractor_explanations.A setting detail: Points to description of place; conflict may arise in a setting but is not itself a detail of it.
distractor_explanations.A type of poem: Misfiles the term under genre; conflict is a narrative element found across all forms of literature.

distractor_explanations.A setting: Names the story's place rather than its central character; protagonists act within the setting.
distractor_explanations.A narrator: Confuses who tells the story with whom it is about; the narrator may or may not be the main character.
distractor_explanations.The villain: Equates importance with opposition; the protagonist leads the story, and the villain may oppose them.

distractor_explanations.Neither matters: Dismisses both concepts; authorial attitude and reader feeling are central to interpreting a text.
distractor_explanations.They are the same: Collapses the distinction; tone belongs to the author's stance, mood to the atmosphere readers feel.
distractor_explanations.Mood is author's; tone is reader's: Reverses the two terms; tone is the author's attitude, and mood is the feeling evoked in the reader.

distractor_explanations.Memorizing word lists: Builds isolated knowledge; words learned through context clues attach to meaningful use and endure.
distractor_explanations.Ignoring vocabulary: Skips the skill entirely; readers grow by working out unfamiliar words from surrounding clues.
distractor_explanations.Looking up every unknown word: Interrupts reading and breeds dependence; inferring meaning from context builds independent word-solving.

distractor_explanations.A punctuation mark: Confuses symbols with marks on the page; symbolism is a meaning-making device, not a mechanical convention.
distractor_explanations.A type of rhyme: Misfiles the term under sound devices; symbolism operates through representation, not repetition of sound.
distractor_explanations.A character name: Points to a single story element; symbolism is the practice of objects or events standing for abstract ideas.

distractor_explanations.To confuse readers: Mistakes puzzle for purpose; the uncertainty invites readers to question and judge, not to feel lost.
distractor_explanations.It is required by convention: Assumes a rule exists; unreliable narration is a deliberate choice for effect, not a formal obligation.
distractor_explanations.Because they don't know how to write: Attributes to incompetence what is craft; skewed narration is engineered to create dramatic irony.

distractor_explanations.A type of poetry: Misfiles the term under genre; imagery is descriptive language found in prose and verse alike.
distractor_explanations.A photograph: Takes the term literally; literary imagery creates pictures in the mind through words, not camera images.
distractor_explanations.A character trait: Points to characterization; imagery describes sensory experience rather than who a character is.

distractor_explanations.All authors have the same purpose: Erases the differences; whether a text informs, persuades, or entertains changes how it should be read.
distractor_explanations.It only affects title: Shrinks purpose to naming; purpose shapes content, structure, and the strategy a reader should adopt.
distractor_explanations.It doesn't matter: Dismisses purpose entirely; identifying intent is what tells readers how to weigh and approach a text.

distractor_explanations.They don't understand vocabulary: Targets word knowledge when the gap is abstraction; retelling plots requires little vocabulary depth.
distractor_explanations.They read too much: Treats practice as the problem; more reading without abstraction work will not produce theme analysis.
distractor_explanations.They need more practice reading: Repeats the same kind of practice; moving from events to universal ideas needs explicit instruction.

distractor_explanations.Showing through actions only: Defines indirect characterization; direct means the author states the trait outright.
distractor_explanations.Character describes themselves: Confuses narrator statement with self-report; direct characterization is the author's explicit telling.
distractor_explanations.Reader infers from dialogue: Describes indirect methods; inference is what direct characterization lets readers skip.

distractor_explanations.Only dialogue matters: Excludes description altogether; dialogue conveys mood alongside, not instead of, atmospheric detail.
distractor_explanations.Mood is unrelated to setting: Denies the connection the question asks about; weather, time, and place are classic mood-builders.
distractor_explanations.Setting has no effect: Repeats the dismissal; the emotional tone of a scene is largely constructed through its setting.

distractor_explanations.Ignoring the distinction: Abandons the very skill to be taught; students must learn to test claims, not overlook them.
distractor_explanations.Reading more texts: Adds volume without a method; exposure alone does not teach students how to verify or judge statements.
distractor_explanations.Memorizing definitions: Stops at recall; the skill lies in applying the test, provable or subjective, to actual sentences.

distractor_explanations.The story's ending: Confuses narrative position with resolution; point of view governs who tells the story throughout.
distractor_explanations.A character's opinion: Mixes up stance in the story with stance on it; point of view is a technical vantage, not a belief.
distractor_explanations.The physical location of characters: Takes 'point' literally as place; point of view is narrative perspective: first, second, or third person.

distractor_explanations.Because the text is badly written: Blames the writing rather than the reading; disagreement stems from differing reader backgrounds.
distractor_explanations.Because one reader is wrong: Assumes meaning must be single; readers legitimately construct different meanings from the same text.
distractor_explanations.Meaning is always objective: Denies the reader's role; interpretation draws on personal experience, so meaning is co-constructed.

distractor_explanations.Publishing: Names the final stage; publishing shares finished work and comes after drafting, revising, and editing.
distractor_explanations.Proofreading: Names a late, mechanics-focused stage; it checks errors only after ideas are drafted and revised.
distractor_explanations.Editing: Jumps to polishing; editing refines existing drafts, which cannot exist before ideas are generated.

distractor_explanations.It wastes class time: Dismisses the activity entirely; evaluating peers' drafts is itself practice in critical reading.
distractor_explanations.Teachers should do all reviewing: Concentrates feedback in one source; peers provide an authentic audience teachers cannot replicate.
distractor_explanations.Students cannot give useful feedback: Underestimates peer capability; even imperfect feedback sharpens both reviewer's and writer's thinking.

distractor_explanations.Sentence length: Targets a surface feature; varying length cannot supply the missing logical links between ideas.
distractor_explanations.Grammar: Targets correctness within sentences; the problem is between sentences, where connections are missing.
distractor_explanations.Spelling: Addresses mechanics at word level; coherence fails at the level of ideas and their relationships.

distractor_explanations.Counting words: Reduces revision to a quota; checklists guide judgments about content and organization, not length.
distractor_explanations.Grading peer work: Confuses self-monitoring with evaluation; the checklist guides the writer's own review, not others' grades.
distractor_explanations.Decorating papers: Mistakes a working tool for presentation; checklists operate during revision, before submission.

distractor_explanations.To decorate an essay: Treats planning as ornament; the outline exists to arrange ideas before drafting begins.
distractor_explanations.To replace writing: Overstates the outline's role; it organizes the plan but is not a substitute for the essay itself.
distractor_explanations.To count words: Reduces planning to measurement; outlines arrange ideas hierarchically, not by quantity.

distractor_explanations.Because editing comes first: Reverses the sequence; generating ideas precedes polishing, which is why the process is not linear.
distractor_explanations.Because there is no process: Confuses recursion with absence of structure; writers cycle through identifiable stages.
distractor_explanations.Because it follows strict steps: Asserts the opposite of recursion; a strict one-way sequence is exactly what writers abandon when they loop back.

distractor_explanations.Allowing phone reading: Lowers engagement rather than building skill; reading from a screen does not teach structured delivery.
distractor_explanations.Having them read from paper: Substitutes recitation for speaking; reading verbatim keeps eyes on text instead of on the audience.
distractor_explanations.Skipping presentations: Removes the practice entirely; speaking skill develops through structured, supported performance.

distractor_explanations.An introduction: Confuses opening moves with closing purpose; a call to action typically ends by urging readers to act.
distractor_explanations.A bibliography entry: Points to citation apparatus; a call to action is a persuasive move, not a reference.
distractor_explanations.A question: Mistakes a rhetorical device for a directive; the call to action tells readers what specifically to do.

distractor_explanations.Waiting to speak: Describes conversational politeness, not listening; attention is on one's own turn, not the message.
distractor_explanations.Listening while doing other tasks: Describes divided attention, the opposite of the concentration active listening requires.
distractor_explanations.Hearing without responding: Stops at reception; active listening includes responding and confirming understanding.

distractor_explanations.Only English teachers need it: Limits writing to one class; every subject asks students to plan, draft, and revise their thinking.
distractor_explanations.Writing is only for language arts: Applies the same narrowing; science labs and history essays also demand organized written communication.
distractor_explanations.Process doesn't matter: Dismisses instruction entirely; unplanned writing produces unorganized communication in any field.

distractor_explanations.A plot summary: Retells what happened; a theme statement says what the events mean about life or human nature.
distractor_explanations.A setting description: Describes where the story unfolds; theme concerns the message, not the place.
distractor_explanations.A character name: Names a single element; a theme statement expresses the work's central idea as a full sentence.

distractor_explanations.Structure doesn't matter: Dismisses organization entirely; readers depend on structure to follow an argument's progression.
distractor_explanations.Structure is decorative: Treats organization as ornament; in expository writing, structure is functional, locating and sequencing ideas.
distractor_explanations.It makes text longer: Confuses organization with expansion; structure arranges content, it does not add to it.

distractor_explanations.Reading speed: Speed is not the gap; the student already reads accurately, so pacing will not build inferencing.
distractor_explanations.Decoding: The stem states decoding is accurate; the breakdown lies in strategy use, not word recognition.
distractor_explanations.Letter recognition: A far earlier skill than this student shows; identifying letters is not where meaning fails.

distractor_explanations.Situational comedy: Confuses irony with humor; dramatic irony may be serious and concerns knowledge asymmetry.
distractor_explanations.Verbal sarcasm: Names verbal irony spoken by a character; dramatic irony lies in what the audience knows.
distractor_explanations.Irony in poetry: Limits the device to one genre; dramatic irony appears in drama and narrative whenever the audience knows more.

distractor_explanations.A factual history: Overstates accuracy; legends grow from historical events but become embellished in retelling.
distractor_explanations.A scientific report: Confuses folklore with empirical documentation; legends are traditional narratives, not studies.
distractor_explanations.A poem: Names a form rather than a story type; legends are defined by content and origin, not verse structure.

distractor_explanations.All words are interchangeable: Assumes synonyms are equivalent; connotation and formality make each word carry a distinct effect.
distractor_explanations.Word choice doesn't matter: Dismisses diction entirely; the specific word chosen shapes tone and precision of meaning.
distractor_explanations.Only syntax matters: Credits arrangement alone; individual word meanings and associations carry meaning independently of order.

distractor_explanations.Memorizing passages: Builds recall, not inference; remembering text verbatim does not teach reading between the lines.
distractor_explanations.Reading faster: Increases pace without deepening processing; inference requires slowing to consider what is suggested.
distractor_explanations.Literal questioning only: Keeps students at surface facts; inference practice must move beyond what the text states directly.

distractor_explanations.A biography: Names a factual account of a life; allegory is a fictional narrative carrying symbolic meaning.
distractor_explanations.A joke: Confuses allegory with humor; the sustained symbolic narrative is the defining feature.
distractor_explanations.A type of rhyme: Misfiles the term under sound devices; allegory operates through symbolic representation, not sound.

distractor_explanations.A character type: Confuses plot device with characterization; a cliffhanger is a situation, not a person.
distractor_explanations.A setting: Names where the story happens; the cliffhanger is an unresolved moment, not a place.
distractor_explanations.A type of poem: Misfiles the term under genre; cliffhangers appear in chapters and episodes across forms.

distractor_explanations.Exaggeration: Defines hyperbole; an oxymoron joins contradictory terms rather than overstating.
distractor_explanations.Comparison with like/as: Defines simile; oxymorons pair opposites such as 'bittersweet' instead of comparing two things.
distractor_explanations.Repetition: Names sound devices like anaphora; oxymorons rely on contradiction, not repeated wording.

distractor_explanations.It is decorative: Treats the thesis as ornament; it is the claim every paragraph of the essay supports.
distractor_explanations.Only needed for fiction: Reverses the context; argumentative writing centers on the thesis, while fiction needs none.
distractor_explanations.Thesis doesn't matter: Dismisses the controlling idea; without a central claim, the argument has no direction to follow.

distractor_explanations.Reading faster: Accelerates a process that is already breaking down at the meaning stage; speed cannot fix comprehension.
distractor_explanations.More decoding practice: Repeats what the student has mastered; word recognition is intact, comprehension strategies are not.
distractor_explanations.Skipping comprehension: Removes the exact skill being taught; avoiding the difficulty leaves the gap unaddressed.

distractor_explanations.Sound repetition: Names alliteration; personification grants human qualities rather than repeating sounds.
distractor_explanations.Exaggeration: Defines hyperbole; personification attributes human traits, it does not inflate scale.
distractor_explanations.Comparison using like/as: Defines simile; no comparison is being drawn when non-human things take on human qualities.

distractor_explanations.Conflict is unnecessary: Removes the engine of story; without opposing forces there is no tension to resolve.
distractor_explanations.Only action matters: Reduces narrative to events; conflict is what makes those events matter to characters and readers.
distractor_explanations.Conflict confuses readers: Misreads tension as disorder; conflict organizes the plot toward its resolution.

distractor_explanations.Skipping unknown words: Trains avoidance; struggling readers most need supported encounters with unfamiliar words.
distractor_explanations.Memorizing word lists: Builds isolated recall; words learned out of context rarely transfer to actual reading.
distractor_explanations.Ignoring vocabulary: Abandons instruction precisely where students struggle; vocabulary gaps compound comprehension failure.

distractor_explanations.Understatement: Names the opposite device; hyperbole inflates for effect while understatement minimizes.
distractor_explanations.Sound repetition: Names alliteration; hyperbole operates through exaggerated claims, not repeated sounds.
distractor_explanations.Comparison with like/as: Defines simile; hyperbole states an impossible magnitude instead of drawing a comparison.

distractor_explanations.Because they forgot chronological order: Attributes to error what is design; flashbacks deliberately step back from the present timeline.
distractor_explanations.Flashbacks are never useful: Rejects the device outright; flashbacks supply background that the present-moment plot cannot.
distractor_explanations.To confuse readers: Mistakes complexity for obfuscation; the shift in time exists to explain current motivations.

distractor_explanations.To fill space: Reduces transitions to padding; each transition encodes a specific logical relationship.
distractor_explanations.Decoration: Treats transitions as ornament; they do the work of connecting ideas for the reader.
distractor_explanations.Transitions are optional: Dismisses the connective tissue; without transitions, relationships between ideas go unstated.

distractor_explanations.All audiences are the same: Assumes one-size-fits-all writing; audiences differ in background knowledge and expectations.
distractor_explanations.Only teachers read student writing: Narrows writing to a school exercise; real writing reaches varied audiences needing adjustment.
distractor_explanations.Audience doesn't matter: Dismisses the reader entirely; tone, evidence, and organization all shift with who is reading.

distractor_explanations.Grammar: Targets sentence-level correctness; the sentences are fine individually, the problem is their fit.
distractor_explanations.Spelling: Addresses word-level mechanics; unrelated sentences fail at the level of topic and relevance.
distractor_explanations.Sentence length: Adjusts a surface feature; length control cannot create relevance to a central topic.

distractor_explanations.A grammatical error: Treats 'hook' as a fault; in writing instruction it names an intentional opening move.
distractor_explanations.A conclusion: Reverses the position; the hook opens the essay, while conclusions wrap it up.
distractor_explanations.A bibliography entry: Points to citation apparatus; a hook is a rhetorical device for capturing reader interest.

distractor_explanations.An introduction: Names the whole opening section; the thesis is a single claim that typically appears within it.
distractor_explanations.A conclusion: Points to the essay's end; the thesis comes early and drives everything after it.
distractor_explanations.A question: Confuses posing an issue with taking a stance; a thesis asserts a claim, it does not ask.

distractor_explanations.Proofreading comes first: Reverses the order; mechanics are checked last, after content and structure are settled.
distractor_explanations.Editing is optional: Removes a necessary stage; content-level revision cannot be skipped in favor of error-checking.
distractor_explanations.They are the same: Collapses two distinct stages; one addresses ideas and organization, the other surface errors.

distractor_explanations.Memorizing definitions: Stops at terminology; appeals are learned by spotting how real speakers deploy them.
distractor_explanations.Reading about rhetoric: Substitutes secondhand description for analysis; students must examine actual texts.
distractor_explanations.Ignoring appeals: Abandons the target skill; identifying ethos, pathos, and logos requires attention, not avoidance.

distractor_explanations.Passive construction: Names the opposite; active voice puts the subject in the acting role.
distractor_explanations.Object performs the action: Describes passive voice; in active voice, the subject acts rather than receives the action.
distractor_explanations.No subject needed: Removes the agent entirely; active voice requires a subject performing the verb's action.

distractor_explanations.Define terms: Names an early-essay move; definitions belong in the introduction, where readers need them.
distractor_explanations.Introduce new ideas: Violates the closing convention; new arguments belong in the body, not the final paragraph.
distractor_explanations.List sources: Confuses the essay's end with its bibliography; sources appear in citations, not the conclusion.

distractor_explanations.Revision is unnecessary: Contradicts the premise; if revision happened at all, the question of cycling back would arise.
distractor_explanations.First draft is always final: Assumes one-pass writing; drafts almost always expose issues that send writers back a stage.
distractor_explanations.Writing has no process: Confuses non-linearity with absence of process; revision follows recognizable, revisitable stages.
